title: The wrong bishop
summary: A bishop and a pawn up and still a draw: when the corner is the wrong colour, the king that gets there saves half a point.
part.corner.title: The corner the bishop cannot reach
part.corner.summary: Black king on h8, light-squared bishop: nothing gets the king out.
part.colour.title: Right bishop, wrong bishop
part.colour.summary: The colour of the promotion square decides everything. With the right bishop, one check is enough.
part.cutoff.title: Shutting the corner's door
part.cutoff.summary: The attacker keeps the king out: the bishop takes g8 and the king takes g7.
part.race.title: The race to the corner
part.race.summary: Standing in front of the pawn is not enough. The king must get into the corner, and sometimes only one path works.
part.sacrifice.title: The saving sacrifice
part.sacrifice.summary: The resource Taimanov missed against Fischer, and why two rook pawns are worth the same as one.
part.summary.title: The summary
part.summary.summary: Three rules and one race played to the end against the machine.
step.t_corner: White is a bishop and a pawn up, and to move. The black king is on h8. Before any calculation: can White win? Look at the colour of the corner and the colour of the bishop.
step.t_corner.hint1: For the pawn to queen, the black king has to leave h8. Who can force it to?
step.t_corner.hint2: h8 is a dark square. The bishop on f1 only moves on light ones.
step.corner: This is the wrong bishop. The h-pawn queens on h8, a dark square, and White's bishop lives on the light squares. It can never check on h8, never control h8. The black king stays there, steps to g8 or h7 and back, and nothing drives it out. With a whole piece more, White can only stalemate.
step.d_corner: I will play White and try everything. Watch what happens to the black king.
step.d_corner.m1: h6. The pawn advances and takes g7 away from the black king.
step.d_corner.m2: The black king goes to g8, no hurry.
step.d_corner.m3: Kg6. Now g7 and h7 are closed.
step.d_corner.m4: Kh8, the only drawing move, and the only one it needs. Had it gone to f8, h7 would follow and the pawn would queen: the black king would never reach the corner again.
step.d_corner.m5: h7, and Black has no move: g8 is covered by the pawn, g7 by the king. Stalemate. A draw.
step.cornerMove: Now you defend with Black. Stay in the corner and do not let the white king into g7.
step.cornerMove.hint: Move only between h8, g8 and h7. Any square outside opens the door.
step.cornerMove.done: That's it. You just swung between h8 and g8, and White cannot make progress without stalemating.
step.t_colour: I changed one thing: the bishop is now on e1, on the dark squares. White to move. Is it still a draw?
step.t_colour.hint1: With this bishop, which square next to the corner can White hit with a check?
step.t_colour.hint2: The dark-squared bishop reaches h8. The black king can be driven out.
step.colour: The rule is to look at the promotion square. h8 is dark: with the dark-squared bishop it checks in the corner and the king must leave; with the light-squared one the king stays forever. On the other side of the board it is the mirror: a8 is light, so the wrong bishop for the a-pawn is the dark-squared one.
step.d_right: With the right bishop, the black king in the corner does not hold. Watch.
step.d_right.m1: Kg6. The white king takes g7 and h7.
step.d_right.m3: h6. No hurry: the pawn comes closer.
step.d_right.m4: The black king goes back to the corner.
step.d_right.m5: Bc3+. This is the check the wrong bishop could never give.
step.d_right.m6: The king has to leave for g8.
step.d_right.m7: h7+, and the king is pushed out.
step.d_right.m9: h8=Q+. The pawn is through. The right bishop made all the difference.
step.aPawn: The same reasoning with the a-pawn. a8 is light, and the bishop on e1 is dark-squared. The black king sits on a8 and never leaves: a8 to b8 and back. Side of the board and pawn do not matter; the colour of the promotion square does.
step.rightMove: White to move and win, with the right bishop. But careful: one natural move here throws it all away.
step.rightMove.hint: h7 now stalemates the black king. First get the king out of the corner with the bishop.
step.rightMove.done: Well done. Bishop check, the pawn pushes the king away and queens. h7 on the first move would have been stalemate.
step.t_cutoff: The bishop is the wrong one again, but the black king is still on f8, outside the corner. White to move. How do you stop it from reaching h8?
step.t_cutoff.hint1: Through which square does the black king want to enter the corner?
step.t_cutoff.hint2: g8 is light. White's bishop can take it.
step.cutoff: If the king gets into the corner, it is a draw. So White's job is to shut the door first. The black king's way in is through g8; g8 is a light square, and the bishop can take it: Bc4! (Kh7 also works). The white king looks after g7 and h7. With both doors shut, the black king stays outside and the pawn walks up.
step.d_cutoff: Watch White shut the door and then bring the pawn home.
step.d_cutoff.m2: The black king has no way in and backs away.
step.d_cutoff.m3: Kg7. The white king settles next to the corner.
step.d_cutoff.m4: The black king tries to come back the long way.
step.d_cutoff.m5: h6. The pawn runs with the king guarding its path.
step.d_cutoff.m7: h7, and the pawn queens next. The door stayed shut the whole time.
step.cutoffMove: White to move and win. Only one move shuts the door. Find it, then take the pawn up to h6.
step.cutoffMove.hint: The white king already takes g7. What is missing is g8: on which diagonal does the bishop reach it?
step.cutoffMove.done: Perfect. Bb3 was the only move: the bishop shuts g8, the king takes g7 and the pawn goes through.
step.t_mednis: Now you defend. Black to move. Your king is in front of the pawn, on h6. Is that enough? Where does it need to be?
step.t_mednis.hint1: If the white king reaches g8 or g7, what happens to your king?
step.t_mednis.hint2: In front of the pawn is not the same as in the corner. Step into it.
step.mednis: Mednis used this position to show an important difference. In the king and rook pawn ending, standing in front of the pawn is enough. Here it is not. If White were to move, Kg8! would shut g7 and h7 next, and the black king would be left outside. With Black to move, Kh7! and, next move, h8. The king must get into the corner, not stand at the door.
step.d_mednis: I will defend with Black. First I get into the corner, then I simply stay.
step.d_mednis.m1: Kh7. The only move: now g8 is within reach.
step.d_mednis.m3: Kh8. I am in the corner.
step.d_mednis.m5: Kh7, and nobody gets me out of here. A draw.
step.raceMove: Black to move and draw. The white king and bishop want to shut the corner. Run to h8 without wasting time.
step.raceMove.hint: Head for g7 along the diagonal. Once the bishop takes h7, the only door left is g7.
step.raceMove.done: That's it. You went along the diagonal and, when the bishop came to c2, Kg7 was the only move. Now the king is home.
step.t_taimanov: Fischer against Taimanov, Vancouver, 1971. Black to move, with a knight against bishop and pawn. The black king is far from h8. Which plan saves Black?
step.t_taimanov.hint1: Think about what happens if the knight disappears from the board. Which ending is left?
step.t_taimanov.hint2: Light-squared bishop and h-pawn: the wrong bishop. The knight can offer itself.
step.taimanov: Here Black does not need the knight. If it leaves the board, what remains is king, light-squared bishop and h-pawn against king: the wrong bishop. So the knight goes to d3 and f4 and offers itself to the king or the bishop; while White spends time on it, the black king runs to h8. Taimanov played Ke4??, left the knight too far away and lost.
step.d_taimanov: The plan that would have saved Taimanov.
step.d_taimanov.m1: Nd3. The knight heads for f4, where it offers itself and watches the pawn.
step.d_taimanov.m2: h4. The pawn tries to run.
step.d_taimanov.m3: Nf4. The knight arrives and covers h5.
step.d_taimanov.m5: Ke5 defends the knight. If White takes it, the black king runs to the corner, and it is the wrong bishop. A draw.
step.twoPawns: And with two h-pawns? Nothing changes. Both queen on h8, which is still dark, and the black king still sits in the corner. With the wrong bishop, extra rook pawns on the same file only add stalemate chances.
step.twoPawnsMove: Black to move and draw, against two h-pawns. Same rule as always.
step.twoPawnsMove.hint: Away from e7 and e8. Your place is near g8 and h8.
step.twoPawnsMove.done: That's it. King in the corner, and the two pawns are worth no more than one.
step.t_finish: The last position is for playing. Black to move. Where does the king go, and by which path?
step.t_finish.hint1: The h8 corner is the goal. Count your king's moves and the white king's moves to g7.
step.recap: Three rules to take to your games. First: look at the colour of the rook pawn's promotion square. If the bishop does not move on it, the king in the corner draws.
step.rules: Second: the attacker shuts the door first, with the bishop covering the square next to the corner (g8) and the king on g7. Third: the defender runs to the corner, not just in front of the pawn, and gives up a piece to get there if needed. Now play the race to the end.
step.finish: Black to move and draw. Take the king to h8 against the machine.
ex.e09: Black to move and draw. Each side has a bishop, of opposite colours, and White has two pawns. Beware of the natural move.
ex.e09.hint: The corner looks safe, but the g-pawn is not a rook pawn. Keep your king watching f7 and g7.
ex.e09.solution: Kf8! Kh8?? loses: 2.Ke6 Kg8 3.Ke7+ Kh8 4.Kf7 and the g-pawn goes through. With the king on f8, the white king cannot reach f7.
key.corner: The basic position: black king on h8, light-squared bishop and h-pawn. A draw, whoever moves. The idea is in the Lichess studies by ibmm and ps503graupera.
key.rightBishop: The same position with the dark-squared bishop: White wins. Lesson position.
key.aPawn: The mirror on the a-pawn: a8 is light, so the dark-squared bishop is the wrong one. A draw (Wikipedia, Fortress).
key.cutoff: Shutting the door: Bc4! takes g8 before the black king gets in. Lesson position.
key.mednis: Mednis's position (via Wikipedia): in front of the pawn is not enough. White to move wins with Kg8! Black to move draws with Kh7!
key.fischerTaimanov: Fischer–Taimanov, Vancouver 1971: 81...Nd3! would have drawn, because without the knight the ending is the wrong bishop. Taimanov played Ke4?? and lost.
history: The idea is old. Wikipedia points to a study by Greco, from 1623, in which Black gives up the bishop to leave White with a rook pawn and the wrong-coloured bishop. The manuals file this ending among the elementary fortresses: Dvoretsky has a section called "Bishop and Rook Pawn", and Müller and Lamprecht one called "Wrong Rook's Pawn". Great players have won and lost by it. In Vancouver, 1971, Taimanov had a knight against Fischer's bishop and h-pawn; offering the knight and running to the corner was enough, but he played Ke4?? and lost. In Baguio, 1978, Korchnoi reached against Karpov an ending with the dark-squared bishop and the a-pawn, the wrong bishop, and the game ended in stalemate on move 124. The tablebase confirms every position in this lesson.
practice: Now against the machine, with White. It is the position from the part on shutting the door: find the move that takes g8 and bring the pawn all the way.
ex.e12: White to play and draw. The black king is already near the corner and the bishop sits on a2. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: a1 is a dark square and Black's bishop is light-squared. Your king needs to reach b1 or a1 before the bishop takes b1.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kc2! The king covers b1, b2 and b3 and stands one step from the corner. After 1...Bb3+ comes 2.Kb1!, and the white king shuttles between b1 and a1: the light-squared bishop never drives it off a1. With 1.Kc3? Bb1! the bishop shuts the door, the black king gets out via b2 and the pawn runs.
ex.e13: White to play and win. The bishop is the wrong one and the black king is running for h8. Which piece shuts the door?
ex.e13.hint: Covering g8 with the bishop is not enough: the black king can walk down the h-file. What covers h7 and h8 at once?
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kf7! (1.Kf8 also works) and, after 1...Kh6, 2.Kg8! (or 2.Bf5, covering h7): the white king holds h7 and h8 and the pawn walks up. The natural 1.Be6? covers g8, but 1...Kh6 and the black king gets in via the h-file, h7 and h8: draw.
ex.e14: Black to play and draw. Your b-pawn is a problem: White wants to trade it and get a b-pawn. Where does the king go?
ex.e14.hint: If a white a-pawn captures onto b6, the bishop is no longer the wrong one. Do not give White time for a5, and do not push your pawn.
ex.e14.solution: 1...Kb8! The king stays one step from a8. If 2.Bxb6, 2...Ka8! and only a-pawns are left with the dark-squared bishop: draw. 1...Ka7? loses to 2.a5! Kxa6 3.axb6, and the b-pawn queens on b8, a dark square. 1...b5? 2.axb5 gives the same b-pawn.
ex.e15: White to play and draw. Trading bishops looks safe, but the pawn ending is lost. There is another way.
ex.e15.hint: If Black's b-pawn turns into an a-pawn, what colour is a1? And which squares does Black's bishop move on?
ex.e15.solution: 1.a5! If 1...bxa5, Black's pawn becomes an a-pawn and Black's bishop is light-squared, the wrong one for a1. Then 2.Kf2!, and the king runs to b1 and a1 in time. If 1...Bxh1, 2.axb6 and Black's bishop is tied to b7: with no black pawn left, it is a draw. 1.Bxd5+? Kxd5 loses: the white king cannot catch the pawns.
ex.e16: White to play and draw, with one pawn against bishop and pawn. A study published on Lichess. Three only moves in a row.
ex.e16.hint: h1 is light and Black's bishop is dark-squared. Your king must get to h1, but the a-pawn can win the tempi it needs.
ex.e16.solution: 1.a6! (the pawn steps out of the black king's reach) 1...Bc5 2.Kc7! 2...h5 3.Kc6! The king covers b5 and threatens Kb7 and a7, so the bishop has to watch a7; after 3...Bg1 4.a7 Bxa7 5.Kd5 the white king is inside the h-pawn's square and reaches h1. Every white move was the only one: 2.Kb7?, for example, arrives one tempo late.
ex.e17: White to play and draw. Bishop and knight against bishop and two pawns, with the white king already on h1. A study published on Lichess.
ex.e17.hint: With the g-pawn, Black's bishop is the right one for g1. Make the g-pawn capture onto the h-file, and for that your bishop has to reach h6 with tempo.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Nd2!! Kxd2 2.Bg5+! Kd1 3.Bh6!! The knight lures the king to d2 so that Bg5 comes with check and the bishop reaches h6 without losing time. If 3...gxh6, Black is left with two h-pawns and the dark-squared bishop, the wrong one for h1. If the g-pawn advances, Bxf8; if the bishop moves away, Bxg7. Either way the white king holds the corner.
